Offered is a copy of Crime SuspenStories #22, published by E.C. Comics with a cover date of April/May 1954. This issue is renowned for the classic Johnny Craig decapitation cover, widely regarded as the most notorious cover of the pre-code era.
Contained within are stories by William Gaines, who famously testified before the 1954 Senate investigation into the influence of comic books on children and teens. During this testimony, Gaines was asked, “Do you consider this to be in good taste?” to which he responded, “Yes, for a horror comic.” This book, often cited as the most infamous in the medium, played a pivotal role in the formation of the Comics Code Authority, making it a historic addition to any comic collection.
Adding to its allure, the interior artwork features contributions from Golden Age legends Bernard Krigstein, Jack Kamen, and Joe Orlando, further enhancing the desirability and historical significance of this already coveted book.

Presented is a 128-card complete set of 1953 Bowman "Frontier Days" collectibles. By 1953, it had become clear that Bowman had lost its dominance over Topps for gum card marketshare. With its fortunes on the wane, it's speculated that the older company made a calculation: We've already commissioned expensive artwork for a successful set ... why not reuse it? So, Bowman tapped the archives, "borrowed" 128 subjects from its 1951 "Wild West" issue, and expanded cards' dimensions to a premium size that was rapidly increasing in popularity. The result was an exciting "new" product—"Frontier Days"—that realized a satisfying amount of success in its own right by featuring a range of Western scenes that retained every bit of their original excitement. This is a notably challenging set to assemble: though the fact isn't widely publicized, veteran hobbyists attest to the relative scarcity of the issue's higher-numbered cards. special_note: Historical significance related to the Beatles' disguise and fan reaction.
description_block:
Reverse stamped caption reads, "IT'S THE BEATLES - DISGUISED AS POLICEMEN - The Beatles gave their fans the slip on Sunday (10-11-63) by dressing up as policemen. They sat in a Black Maria which was driven past hundreds of screaming fans and through the side gates of a theatre. When the girl fans realized they had been fooled they rushed the gates. Police struggled to hold them back. One officer had his hand crushed as he helped to close the gates. But by that time the Beatles, wearing helmets and dark coats, had been smuggled in by the stage door. The Beat-the-Beatlemania campaign went into operation for the Liverpool group's one-night stand at Birmingham Hippodrome. Earlier, the Beatles' car had broken down on the M1 on its way from London. After repairs, the group drove to Birmingham's police headquarters for briefing. Said guitarist George Harrison: 'They put us in the Black Maria and told us to put helmets on. We didn't really need them, but it was great fun. The police seemed to enjoy it as much as we did.' Special reward for the helpful policemen - the Beatles' autographs."

description_block:
Graded 8.5 with an H-seam seal rating of B+ by WATA Games (576733-001). This 3-Screw cart copy bears a Rev-A label, USA Code, and an oval Nintendo SoQ R.

Raphael, Donatello, Michealangelo, and Leonardo returned to the Nintendo Entertainment System for the third time in this offered 1992 copy of Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles III: The Manhattan Project developed and published by Konami for release on the NES in February, 1992. The side-scrolling beat 'em-up game takes the high-stakes action and game mechanics from the franchise's second installment, but it is an original title in its own right. The game sees the "Heroes in a Halfshell" vacationing in Key West when they are stirred to action by Shreddar, who has kidnapped April O'Neil and turned Manhattan into a floating island. Featuring single-player and multiplayer action, the game earned Best NES Game of 1992 by Electronic Gaming Monthly.

description_block:
To put a finer point on it, the 35 signatures appear to originate from a postwar reunion of Battery E (Easy), 13th Regiment, 5th Marine Division. Included are sergeants, corporals and privates, among them one Harold Stine who was awarded a bronze star with valor. The 5th Division went into combat for the first time on Iwo Jima and fought there from Feb. 19 to Mar. 26, with 2,500 soldiers killed and over 6,000 wounded. Notably, all 6 of the flag raisers on Mt. Suribachi, as immortalized by AP photographer Joe Rosenthal, were also 5th Marine Division.
Last year, Goldin auctioned a Rosenthal-signed Type I photo for more than $100,000 (linked here). Presented here is the next best thing--a beautiful Type III example printed shortly after the historic battle, yet developed from a copy negative rather than the original negative. PSA/DNA's LOA reads, "Photo is a syndicated example that was made by Press Association from a duplicate negative featuring the Pulitzer Prize shot originally taken by Joe Rosenthal of the Associated Press."
